significance.justification: Verified true, the claim would establish that multilingual LLMs contain a compact, causally active "negation direction" shared across languages, while negative-concord and multi-marker constructions systematically disrupt that operator; this combines a form-(iii) typology-to-error ordering with a form-(ii) causal steering claim. It would establish both a behavioral phenomenon and a mechanism, fixing expectations that negative-concord languages should incur more scope or double-negation errors and that manipulating the shared representation should flip or repair polarity; this bears directly on whether language-neutral representations such as those studied in Wendler et al.'s 2024 "Do Llamas Work in English?" extend from semantic content to logical operations. The branches are distinguishable despite mildly vague terms such as "largely shared": finding language-specific directions or no typology-graded errors would rule out the proposed shared-operator explanation, although refuting only the steering component would be less decisive. The topic-substitution check passes because deleting the specific negation operator, typological ordering, and causal repair leaves only the generic shared-versus-language-specific question, which would not merit this score.

reach.justification: The concrete handles are the "shared negation direction," the typology-graded error relationship, and an intervention that can "flip polarity" or "repair negation-typology-induced errors." The typology relationship supplies limited ex-ante lead time by flagging negative-concord and multi-marker constructions as higher-risk before deployment, while the steering direction is an inference-time control rather than merely a post-hoc explanation. Although the direction itself would require re-extraction for each model, the asserted relation predicts that a shared low-rank polarity representation and greater typological interference should recur across multilingual model families and tasks; likely users include interpretability researchers and practitioners auditing or controlling open-weight multilingual systems, but not clearly researchers outside AI. The topic-substitution check passes because the actionable polarity direction, risk ordering, and steering knob disappear when the claim is reduced to the assigned multilingual-representation topic.
